transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I’m here because my eating has gotten really out of hand. Most nights, after my wife goes to bed, I end up in the kitchen eating way more than a normal meal. Like fried chicken, mac and cheese, sweet potatoes, rolls—whatever leftovers are around. Sometimes it feels like a whole tray is gone, or half the fridge, before I stop.
When you're eating like this, do you feel like you can't stop or control what you're doing?

Yes. Once I take that first bite, it feels like the decision’s already been made. I’ll be telling myself, “George, stop now,” but my hands just keep making another plate or opening another container anyway.
Does this eating behavior bother you or cause problems in your life, like with your health, relationships, or daily activities?

Yes, it does. I’ve kind of pulled back from things I used to be involved in, like community planning meetings and helping with events. I feel embarrassed and worn out, and I worry people can tell I’m not holding things together like I used to.
After these episodes of eating a lot, do you ever try to compensate by doing things like making yourself vomit, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising a lot more than usual?
I’m not really sure. I don’t think I do those kinds of things regularly. Afterward I mostly just feel bad and try to move on, but I don’t have a set thing I do to “make up for it.”
Can you tell me more about how this eating behavior has affected your daily life or the way you feel about yourself?

It’s really changed how I see myself. Afterward I feel sick with myself, honestly. People tend to see me as organized, strong, like I’ve got things handled, and then I’m sitting there ashamed and guilty, disgusted that I let it happen again. It makes me feel like I’m not the person everyone thinks I am.
Have you noticed these eating episodes affecting your ability to function in your usual roles, like at work, at home, or in your community activities?

Yeah. I’ve stopped going to a lot of the community planning meetings, and I don’t help with events like I used to. I just feel embarrassed and drained, and I’m worried people will notice I’m not keeping things together the way I used to.
When you have these episodes of eating a lot, are they related to how you feel about your body shape or weight—like if you feel upset or focused on those things before or after eating?

I’m not sure. I mean, I don’t think it starts because I’m focused on my weight or anything like that. Afterward I might feel bad about myself in general, but I haven’t really connected it specifically to my body shape or weight.

Do you ever feel so upset or overwhelmed by these eating episodes that you have trouble functioning during the day, like difficulty concentrating, feeling too ashamed to interact with others, or taking longer to get things done?

Yeah, I do. After it happens I feel embarrassed and just worn out, and it makes it hard to show up like I normally would. I’ve pulled back from the community planning meetings and helping with events because I’m afraid people will notice I’m not holding things together the way I used to.
Do these episodes ever affect your ability to function at home or work the next day, such as making it hard to concentrate, complete tasks, or interact with family or coworkers?

Yeah, it does. I’m not working right now, but the next day I’ll feel embarrassed and really drained. I’ve pulled back from community planning meetings and helping with events because I’m worried people can tell I’m not holding things together like I used to.
When you’re in the middle of one of these eating episodes, do you feel like you’re not in control of what or how much you’re eating?
Yeah. Once I start, it feels like I’ve already lost the choice somehow. I’ll be telling myself, George, stop, that’s enough, but I keep reaching for more or making another plate anyway.
Outside of avoiding community activities, do these eating episodes cause any other problems in your daily life, such as difficulties with your family, trouble sleeping, or physical discomfort?

I’m not really sure. I mean, besides pulling back from those activities, I haven’t noticed a clear pattern with family or sleep or anything like that. Mostly I just feel bad afterward, but I don’t know if there’s more than that.
When you're having one of these eating episodes, do you find yourself eating much more quickly than normal, or eating until you feel uncomfortably full?

Yeah, I do eat a lot faster than normal. Sometimes I’m standing at the counter just taking big bites and swallowing before I’ve even really chewed the last one. It’s like I barely taste the food, even stuff I used to really care about cooking.
Over the past few months, has this pattern of eating like this happened, on average, at least once a week?
Yeah. For the last few months, I honestly can’t think of a week where it didn’t happen at least once. Most weeks it’s more than that—usually several nights, after my wife’s gone to bed.
Do these eating episodes cause you any physical discomfort, such as stomachaches, nausea, or fatigue the next day?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t really pay close attention to whether I feel sick the next day. Sometimes I just feel kind of lousy afterward, but I can’t say I’ve noticed a clear stomachache or nausea pattern.
Do you feel a lot of distress or emotional pain specifically about these episodes of eating?

Yes. That’s probably the worst part. Afterward I feel sick with myself—ashamed and guilty, like I let it happen again. People see me as organized, like I have things together, but then I’m sitting there feeling disgusted with myself.
Do you usually eat alone during these episodes because you're embarrassed about how much you're eating?
I’m not totally sure it’s because I’m embarrassed, exactly. I do tend to be by myself when it happens, but I haven’t really thought through the reason like that.
